H1.text: Ice melts on a warm afternoon. The same water freezes in a freezer. One change, two directions.

H2.text: Only the temperature changed. So temperature must have a vote.

H3.text: Aarav drops ice into his water bottle in the college corridor. In minutes, it melts.

H4.text: Last time, we had to count the surroundings too. That is hard.

H5.text: By the end, you will know one number about the reaction alone that predicts its direction, and where it stops.

P1.text: Think of a tug of war with two teams.

P2.text: Team one is enthalpy. Giving out heat pulls a change forward.

P3.text: Team two is entropy. More disorder pulls it forward too.

P4.text: Temperature is a booster for team two. The hotter it gets, the harder entropy pulls.

S1.text: Let's put ice on our molecule bench and turn the temperature knob.

S2.text: Melting takes heat in. Plus six kilojoules per mole. Team enthalpy pulls back.

S3.text: But melting makes the water messier. Plus twenty two joules per kelvin per mole. Team entropy pulls forward.

S4.text: At minus ten degrees, enthalpy wins. The ice stays.

S5.text: Turn the knob up. At zero degrees, two seventy three kelvin, the teams are exactly equal. Ice and water sit together.

S6.text: At twenty five degrees, entropy wins. The ice melts.

L1.text: The score of this tug of war is the Gibbs energy, named after Josiah Willard Gibbs.

L2.text: Delta G equals delta H minus T delta S.

L3.text: If delta G is negative, the change is spontaneous. If positive, it is not. If zero, the system is at equilibrium.

D1.text: Why does this work? Step by step.

D2.text: Step one. The total entropy is the system's change plus the surroundings' change.

D3.text: Step two. The surroundings gain the heat the system gives out. Their change is minus delta H over T.

D4.text: Step three. Multiply everything by minus T. Minus T delta S total equals delta H minus T delta S. That is delta G.

D5.text: So total entropy going up means delta G going down. One rule, seen from the system.

G2.text: Heat out and more disorder. Both teams pull forward. Spontaneous at every temperature.

G3.text: Heat in and less disorder. Both pull back. Never spontaneous.

G4.text: Heat out but less disorder. Spontaneous only when cold, like freezing.

G5.text: Heat in but more disorder. Spontaneous only when hot, like melting.

C1.text: Compare. Freezing water: heat out, less disorder. Melting ice: heat in, more disorder.

K1.text: Pause and think. Melting ice at fifty degrees Celsius. Is delta G positive or negative?

K2.text: Negative. Fifty degrees is above two seventy three kelvin, so the entropy team wins.

R2.text: The standard Gibbs energy change tells us how far a reaction goes, through the equilibrium constant K.

R3.text: Delta G naught equals minus R T times the natural log of K. Or minus two point three oh three R T log K, in base ten.

R4.text: R is the gas constant, eight point three one four joules per kelvin per mole.

R5.text: A big negative delta G naught means a huge K. Mostly products. A big positive one means a tiny K. Mostly reactants.

T1.text: Remember this. Negative delta G, spontaneous. Zero, equilibrium.

W2.text: Oxygen turning into ozone at two ninety eight kelvin has K equal to two point four seven times ten to the minus twenty nine. Find delta G naught.

W3.text: Log of K is about minus twenty eight point six oh seven.

W4.text: Two point three oh three, times eight point three one four, times two ninety eight. About five seven oh six joules per mole.

W5.text: Multiply by minus twenty eight point six oh seven, with the minus sign in front. Plus one sixty three kilojoules per mole.

W6.text: Hugely positive, so K is tiny. Oxygen hardly turns into ozone on its own.

X2.text: Students put delta H in kilojoules and delta S in joules straight into the formula.

X3.text: Convert first. Six kilojoules is six thousand joules. Then subtract.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Boards ask what the sign of delta G means. Entrance tests ask the temperature where a reaction turns spontaneous, or ask for K.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A reaction has delta H plus one seventy eight kilojoules per mole and delta S plus one sixty joules per kelvin per mole. Above what temperature is it spontaneous? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. About eleven hundred thirteen kelvin.

A2.text: It becomes spontaneous when delta G drops below zero. Set delta H equal to T delta S.

A3.text: Convert. One seventy eight kilojoules is one lakh seventy eight thousand joules.

A4.text: T equals one seventy eight thousand divided by one sixty. Eleven twelve point five kelvin. A forgot to convert.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. What does a negative delta G tell you?

Y3.text: Two. Why does melting ice need a high enough temperature?

Y4.text: Three. If delta G naught is large and negative, is K big or small?

N1.text: Next time: a reaction reaches equilibrium. Does it really stop, or keep running both ways? We find out in Chapter six, Equilibrium.
